decks.title: Transpiration — Part 1: The process, stomata and experiments
goals: Define transpiration, name its routes and explain its importance
Explain the opening and closing of stomata by potassium ion exchange
Describe the loss-of-weight, bell jar and cobalt chloride paper experiments

slides.heading: Transpiration
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how plants lose water vapour, how stomata open and close, and how we show it.

visual.alt: Flow: roots absorb water, xylem carries it up to the leaf cells, and water vapour escapes through the stomata into the air

slides.narration: A large tree can lift hundreds of litres of water from the soil in a single summer day, and almost all of it escapes from the leaves as invisible vapour. This loss is called transpiration. Let us see where the water goes, why it matters and how we can show it happening.

slides.heading: What is transpiration?
slides.body_md: **Transpiration** is the loss of water as **vapour** from the aerial parts of a plant.

visual.alt: Table of three routes of transpiration: stomata lose most, the cuticle a small amount and lenticels very little

slides.narration: Water evaporates from the moist walls of the leaf cells into the air spaces, then diffuses out mainly through the tiny pores called stomata. A little also escapes through the waxy cuticle and through lenticels in the bark of woody stems.

slides.heading: Why transpiration matters

rows: Draws water and minerals up the xylem from the roots
Evaporation takes away heat from the leaves
Carries minerals to all parts of the shoot
Can cause wilting if loss exceeds uptake: a necessary evil

visual.alt: Table of the effects of transpiration and how each helps or harms the plant

slides.narration: Transpiration is called a necessary evil. It wastes most of the water a plant takes in, and on hot days can make it wilt. But it also pulls water and minerals up to the leaves and cools them, just as sweating cools us.

slides.heading: The stomatal apparatus
slides.body_md: Each **stoma** is a pore between two bean-shaped **guard cells**, which have **chloroplasts** and a **thick inner wall**.

slides.narration: Look closely at a stoma. Two kidney shaped guard cells face each other. Their walls next to the pore are thick, their outer walls thin. When the guard cells swell, the thin walls stretch more, the cells bow apart and the pore opens. When they shrink, the pore closes.

slides.heading: Potassium ion exchange
slides.body_md: In **light**, potassium ions enter the guard cells; in **darkness** they leave.

visual.alt: Flow: light, potassium ions enter the guard cells, water enters by osmosis, the guard cells become turgid, the stoma opens

slides.narration: In light, potassium ions move into the guard cells from the cells around them. The guard cells now hold more dissolved substances, so water flows in by osmosis. They become turgid and the pore opens. At night the ions move out, water follows, and the pore closes.

slides.heading: Quick check: the pore
slides.body_md: Which lettered part lets water vapour escape?
slides.narration: Look for the opening between the two guard cells.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how much water is lost?
slides.body_md: A potted plant absorbed **500 mL** of water in a day and kept only **6 mL**.
bullets: Step 1: water lost = 500 − 6 = **494 mL**.
Step 2: percentage = 494 ÷ 500 × 100 = **98.8 per cent**.
Step 3: conclude: almost all the water absorbed is lost by transpiration.

visual.alt: Worked table: of 500 millilitres absorbed, 6 were kept and 494 lost

slides.narration: Subtract what the plant keeps from what it absorbs, then turn the answer into a percentage. Nearly ninety nine parts in every hundred are lost. That is why measuring water uptake gives a good estimate of transpiration.

slides.heading: Quick check: which ions?
slides.body_md: Fill in: stomata open when ______ ions enter the guard cells.
slides.narration: The element with the symbol K.

slides.heading: Factors affecting transpiration

rows: Faster evaporation; air holds more vapour
Less difference in moisture between leaf and air
Moist air around the leaf is blown away
Stomata close when the plant is short of water

visual.alt: Table of five factors, their effect on the rate of transpiration and the reason

slides.narration: Bright, hot, dry and windy conditions make plants lose water fastest. Dark, cool, humid and still conditions slow it down. Each factor works by changing either the opening of stomata or how easily water vapour can diffuse away.

slides.heading: Adaptations that reduce water loss

rows: Very little surface for water loss
Moist air trapped above the pore
Fewer stomata, mostly on the lower surface
Less exposure to sun and wind
Leaf fall in the dry season

visual.alt: Table of five adaptations that reduce water loss, with examples and how each helps

slides.narration: Desert plants are experts at saving water. A cactus has spines instead of leaves and a waxy green stem. Others hide their stomata in pits or roll their leaves. Many trees simply drop their leaves when water is scarce.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: predicting the rate
slides.body_md: A potometer is carried from a bright, dry, breezy balcony into a dark, steamy bathroom.
bullets: Step 1: **dark**: stomata close, rate falls.
Step 2: **humid** and **still** air: diffusion slows, rate falls.
Step 3: all factors act together: the bubble **slows down greatly**.

visual.alt: Worked table comparing light, humidity and wind on a balcony and in a bathroom, each lowering the rate

slides.narration: Take one factor at a time and decide whether it raises or lowers the rate. Here every factor lowers it, so the prediction is easy. When factors pull in opposite directions, say which one is likely to matter most.

slides.heading: Guttation and bleeding

rows: Hydathodes at leaf tips and margins

visual.alt: Table comparing transpiration, guttation and bleeding in form, place, time and cause

slides.narration: On humid mornings you may see beads of water on the tips of grass blades. This is guttation, pushed out by root pressure through special pores called hydathodes. Bleeding is different: it is sap oozing from a cut or wounded part of a plant.

slides.heading: Quick check: guttation drops
slides.body_md: True or false: the liquid of guttation is pure water.
slides.narration: What does root pressure push up from the soil along with water?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Ganong's potometer measures water uptake, which approximates transpiration.
Light, heat and wind increase transpiration; humidity decreases it.
Desert plants reduce water loss with spines, thick cuticles and sunken stomata.
Guttation: liquid through hydathodes; bleeding: sap from wounds.

visual.alt: Summary table: bright, hot, dry and windy conditions give a high rate; dark, cool, humid and still give a low rate

slides.narration: To recap. The potometer lets us measure water uptake and test the factors. Hot, dry, windy, bright conditions speed transpiration up. Desert plants slow it down. And guttation and bleeding are two other ways water leaves a plant.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: A potometer measures **uptake**, not loss: say "approximately".
For a factor, give the **effect** and the **reason**.
Guttation: **liquid**, **hydathodes**, **root pressure**.
Name a **precaution** for the potometer: cut under water, airtight joints.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Say the potometer measures uptake, so it is only approximate. Give a reason with every factor. Link guttation with liquid, hydathodes and root pressure. And always add the potometer precautions.

notes.title: Transpiration — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Transpiration and its importance
sections.body_md:
**Transpiration** is the loss of water in the form of **vapour** from the aerial parts of a plant. Water evaporates from the moist cell walls of the leaf into the air spaces and diffuses out.

**Types (by route):** **stomatal** (through stomata; most of the loss), **cuticular** (through the cuticle; small), **lenticular** (through lenticels in bark; very little).

Almost all the water absorbed is lost this way (for example, a plant that absorbs 500 mL and keeps 6 mL loses 98.8 per cent).

**Importance:** creates the **transpiration pull** that lifts water and dissolved **minerals** through the xylem; **cools** the leaves; distributes minerals. Because it also wastes water and can cause **wilting**, it is called a **necessary evil**.

key_terms.definition_md: Loss of water as vapour from the aerial parts of a plant.
The pull on the water columns in the xylem created by evaporation from leaves.

visual.alt: Table of the three routes of transpiration and their share

sections.heading: 2. Opening and closing of stomata: potassium ion exchange
sections.body_md:
A **stoma** is a pore surrounded by two bean-shaped **guard cells**, which (unlike other epidermal cells) contain **chloroplasts**. Their **inner walls** (towards the pore) are **thick**; their outer walls are thin.

**Opening (light):** **potassium ions (K+)** move from the neighbouring epidermal cells **into** the guard cells → solute concentration rises → **water enters by osmosis** → guard cells become **turgid** → thin outer walls stretch more, the cells curve apart → **pore opens**.

**Closing (dark, or when the plant is short of water):** K+ ions move **out** → water leaves by osmosis → guard cells become **flaccid** and straight → **pore closes**.

key_terms.definition_md: Bean-shaped cells with chloroplasts that surround a stoma and control its opening.
Swollen and firm because of water taken in.

sections.heading: 3. Experiments on transpiration
sections.body_md:
**Loss of weight:** two flasks of water, each with a **layer of oil** (to stop evaporation): A with a leafy shoot, B with a leafless shoot. Weigh at the start and after some hours. A loses much more weight (for example 11.2 g against 0.8 g in 8 hours). **Conclusion:** water is lost mainly through the leaves. A potted plant with its pot and soil wrapped in polythene can be weighed in the same way.

**Bell jar:** a watered potted plant with its **pot and soil covered in polythene**, under a bell jar on a glass plate; **control**: a covered pot without a plant. **Observation:** drops of water on the inner wall of the jar with the plant only (they turn dry cobalt chloride paper pink). **Conclusion:** the plant gives off water vapour.

**Cobalt chloride paper on a dorsiventral leaf:** dry **blue** paper on both surfaces, covered with glass slides and clipped. **Observation:** the paper on the **lower surface turns pink first**. **Conclusion:** more water is lost from the lower surface, which has **more stomata**. (On an isobilateral leaf such as maize both papers change at about the same time.)

key_terms.definition_md: Paper that is blue when dry and turns pink when it absorbs moisture.
Leaf with distinct upper and lower surfaces; most stomata on the lower surface.

sections.heading: 4. Ganong's potometer
sections.body_md:
A **potometer** measures the **rate of water uptake** by a leafy shoot. The shoot is fitted with an **airtight cork** into a water-filled apparatus; an **air bubble** in a **graduated capillary** moves towards the shoot as water is taken up. A **reservoir** with a stopcock resets the bubble.

**Precautions:** cut the shoot **under water** (no air in the xylem); make all joints **airtight** with Vaseline; keep conditions steady.

**Why it approximates transpiration:** nearly all the water absorbed is lost by transpiration.

**Limitations:** it measures **uptake, not loss**; it uses a **cut shoot**, not a whole plant; air leaks and **temperature changes** affect the bubble.

key_terms.definition_md: Apparatus that measures the rate of water uptake by a cut leafy shoot.

sections.heading: 5. Factors affecting transpiration; adaptations
sections.body_md:
| Factor | Effect | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Light | Increases | Stomata open |
| Temperature | Increases | Faster evaporation |
| Humidity | Decreases | Less difference in moisture between leaf and air |
| Wind | Increases | Moist air around the leaf is removed |
| Soil water | Shortage decreases it | Stomata close |

**Adaptations to reduce transpiration:** leaves reduced to **spines** (Opuntia); **thick waxy cuticle**; **sunken stomata**; fewer stomata, mostly on the lower surface; hairs or rolled leaves; shedding leaves in the dry season.

key_terms.definition_md: Drooping of leaves when water loss exceeds uptake.
Stomata in pits that trap moist air.

visual.alt: Table: hot, dry, windy and bright conditions give a high rate; cool, humid, still and dark give a low rate

sections.heading: 6. Guttation and bleeding
sections.body_md:
**Guttation:** loss of water as **liquid drops** (containing dissolved salts) through **hydathodes** at the tips and margins of leaves, at **night or early morning** when **root pressure is high** and transpiration is low; for example grasses, tomato, garden nasturtium.

**Bleeding:** oozing of **sap** from a **cut or injured** part of a plant, due to root pressure.

| Transpiration | Guttation |
|---|---|
| Water vapour | Liquid drops with salts |
| Through stomata (mainly) | Through hydathodes |
| Mostly by day | Night and early morning |

key_terms.definition_md: Loss of liquid water through hydathodes.
Pore at the leaf tip or margin through which guttation occurs.
Oozing of sap from a cut or injured part of a plant.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing "water" instead of "water vapour" for transpiration.
- Saying potassium ions leave the guard cells when stomata open.
- Forgetting the control (no plant) or the polythene cover in the bell jar experiment.
- Saying a potometer measures transpiration exactly.
- Mixing up guttation (hydathodes, liquid) and bleeding (wounds, sap).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term, a colour change, an odd one out **with its category**.
- 2 marks: a precaution with its reason, or two differences.
- 3 marks: the stomatal mechanism in steps, an experiment (set-up, observation, conclusion), or three factors with reasons.

questions.stem_md: Transpiration is the loss of water

options.text_md: as liquid drops from the margins of leaves
as sap from a cut stem
from the roots into the soil
as water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant

questions.solution_md: Transpiration is evaporation of water, as vapour, mainly through the stomata of leaves — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Most of the water lost in transpiration escapes through the

options.text_md: cuticle
lenticels
stomata
hydathodes

questions.solution_md: Stomatal transpiration accounts for most of the loss; the cuticle and lenticels lose only a little — option (c).

questions.stem_md: On a hot afternoon, water rises to the top leaves of a tall tree mainly because

options.text_md: root pressure pushes it up every hour
the phloem pumps it upwards
the leaves absorb water from the air
evaporation from the leaves creates a pull on the columns of water in the xylem

questions.solution_md: Transpiration pull draws water up through the xylem from the roots — option (d).

questions.stem_md: On a very hot day, the leaves of a well-watered plant stay cooler than a metal plate placed in the same sunshine. This is because

options.text_md: leaves reflect all the sunlight
leaves have no blood to carry heat
the evaporation of water from the leaves takes away heat
the metal plate makes its own heat

questions.solution_md: Evaporation absorbs heat (latent heat), so transpiration cools the leaf — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A potted plant absorbed 500 mL of water in a day and kept only 6 mL in its cells and in photosynthesis. What percentage of the absorbed water was lost by transpiration?
questions.solution_md: Water lost: 500 − 6 gives 494 mL. Percentage: $\dfrac{494}{500} \times 100 = 98.8$ per cent.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Transpiration is often called a necessary evil.

**Reason (R):** Transpiration wastes much of the water a plant absorbs, but it also cools the leaves and draws water and minerals upwards.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and its harmful water loss together with its useful effects is exactly why it is called a necessary evil — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the loss of water in the form of vapour from the aerial parts of a plant.

answer.model_answer_md: **Transpiration.**

questions.solution_md: Transpiration.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Stomata, Cuticle, Lenticels, Root hairs.

answer.model_answer_md: **Root hairs**; the others are **routes through which water is lost in transpiration**.

questions.solution_md: Root hairs absorb water.

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which transpiration is useful to a plant.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It creates a **transpiration pull** that draws **water and dissolved minerals** up from the roots through the xylem.
2. Evaporation of water **cools the leaves** in hot sunshine.

questions.solution_md: Transpiration pull; cooling.

questions.stem_md: According to the potassium ion exchange theory, stomata open when

options.text_md: potassium ions leave the guard cells, making them flaccid
the guard cells lose water to the epidermal cells
potassium ions enter the guard cells and water follows by osmosis, making them turgid
the thick inner walls of the guard cells stretch more than the outer walls

questions.solution_md: K+ entry raises the solute concentration of the guard cells; water enters and they swell and curve apart — option (c).

questions.stem_md: When guard cells become turgid, the stomatal pore opens because

options.text_md: their thin outer walls stretch more than their thick inner walls, so the cells curve apart
their thick inner walls stretch more than the outer walls
the epidermal cells push them apart
the pore is pulled open by the chloroplasts

questions.solution_md: Unequal thickening makes the swelling cells bow outwards, pulling the inner walls apart — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Stomata of most plants close at night because

options.text_md: potassium ions move out of the guard cells and water follows, making them flaccid
potassium ions move into the guard cells
the guard cells take in water at night
the cuticle covers the pores at night

questions.solution_md: In darkness K+ leaves the guard cells, water leaves by osmosis and the cells straighten, closing the pore — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the figure, which letter marks the opening through which water vapour escapes from the leaf?

options.text_md: A
C
B
D

questions.solution_md: B is the stomatal pore. A is a guard cell, C a chloroplast, D the thick inner wall and E an epidermal cell — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Guard cells contain chloroplasts, unlike the other cells of the epidermis.

**Reason (R):** Guard cells open and close the stomatal pore.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but controlling the pore does not by itself explain the presence of chloroplasts — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Stomata close when potassium ions move into the guard cells.

**Reason (R):** Water moves by osmosis towards a region of higher solute concentration.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is false: K+ entry makes guard cells turgid and opens stomata. The reason is true — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The opening of stomata in light is linked to the entry of ______ ions into the guard cells.
questions.solution_md: Potassium (K+) ions.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the pair of bean-shaped cells that surround a stomatal pore.

answer.model_answer_md: **Guard cells.**

questions.solution_md: Guard cells.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: the wall of a guard cell facing the pore is thicker than its outer wall.

answer.model_answer_md: When the cell becomes **turgid**, the thin outer wall **stretches more**, so the cell **curves outwards** and the pore **opens**.

questions.solution_md: Unequal stretching opens the pore.

marking_scheme.step: Thin wall stretches more; cell curves; pore opens

questions.stem_md: Explain the potassium ion exchange theory of the opening and closing of stomata.

answer.model_answer_md: In **light**, **potassium ions** move from the neighbouring epidermal cells **into the guard cells**. Their solute concentration rises, so **water enters by osmosis**, the guard cells become **turgid**, curve apart and the pore **opens**. In **darkness** potassium ions move **out**, water follows, the guard cells become **flaccid** and the pore **closes**.

questions.solution_md: K+ in, water in, turgid: open. K+ out, water out, flaccid: closed.

marking_scheme.step: K+ enters guard cells in light
Water follows by osmosis; turgid; pore opens
Reverse in dark; flaccid; pore closes

questions.stem_md: Draw a neat, labelled diagram of an open stoma in surface view. Label the guard cell, stomatal pore, chloroplast and epidermal cell.

answer.model_answer_md: Two **bean-shaped guard cells** facing each other with a lens-shaped **stomatal pore** between them; small **chloroplasts** and a nucleus in each guard cell; thick inner walls; irregular **epidermal cells** around them.

questions.solution_md: Labelled stoma.

marking_scheme.step: Two guard cells with a pore between
Chloroplasts and thick inner walls shown

questions.stem_md: Dry cobalt chloride paper is

options.text_md: blue, and turns pink when it absorbs water vapour
pink, and turns blue when it absorbs water vapour
white, and turns blue when it absorbs water vapour
green, and turns yellow in light

questions.solution_md: Anhydrous cobalt chloride is blue; the hydrated salt is pink — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the cobalt chloride paper experiment on a dorsiventral leaf, the paper on the lower surface turns pink first because the lower surface

options.text_md: receives more sunlight
has many more stomata than the upper surface
has a thicker cuticle
has no stomata at all

questions.solution_md: More stomata on the lower surface means faster loss of water vapour there — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In the bell jar experiment, the pot and soil are wrapped in polythene in order to

options.text_md: keep the roots warm
stop the plant from absorbing water
let more light reach the leaves
stop water evaporating from the soil and pot, so that all the moisture collected comes from the plant

questions.solution_md: Without the cover, evaporation from the soil would also mist the jar and spoil the result — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In the loss-of-weight experiment, a layer of oil is poured over the water in the flask to

options.text_md: provide food for the shoot
stop water evaporating from the water surface
keep the shoot upright
make the leaves lose more water

questions.solution_md: Oil seals the surface, so any loss in weight is due to the shoot alone — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which is the best control for the bell jar experiment on transpiration?

options.text_md: An identical set-up with a covered pot of soil but no plant
The same plant kept in a dark room without a bell jar
A second plant with its pot left uncovered
A bell jar with a bowl of water in it

questions.solution_md: The control differs only in the absence of the plant, so any moisture difference must be due to the plant — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A flask with a leafy shoot weighed 250.0 g at 9 a.m. and 238.8 g at 5 p.m. Find the average rate of water loss in grams per hour.
questions.solution_md: Loss: 250.0 − 238.8 gives 11.2 g in 8 hours. Rate: $11.2 \div 8 = 1.4$ g per hour.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Cobalt chloride papers clipped to both surfaces of a maize (isobilateral) leaf turn pink at about the same time.

**Reason (R):** An isobilateral leaf has stomata in roughly equal numbers on both surfaces.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the equal distribution of stomata is why both papers change together — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Name the chemical paper that turns from blue to pink when it absorbs water vapour.

answer.model_answer_md: **Cobalt chloride paper.**

questions.solution_md: Cobalt chloride paper.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Bell jar, Cobalt chloride paper, Potometer, Iodine solution.

answer.model_answer_md: **Iodine solution**; the others are **used in experiments on transpiration**.

questions.solution_md: Iodine is used in the starch test.

questions.stem_md: Describe briefly how you would show that a potted plant gives off water vapour, using a bell jar. State what you would observe.

answer.model_answer_md: Water a potted plant, **cover the pot and soil with polythene**, and place it under a **bell jar** on a glass plate in sunlight, with a control set-up having no plant. After a few hours **drops of water** collect on the **inner wall** of the jar with the plant, but not in the control.

questions.solution_md: Set-up and observation.

marking_scheme.step: Set-up with covered pot and control
Drops inside the jar with the plant only

questions.stem_md: A potometer directly measures

options.text_md: the rate of photosynthesis
the rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot
the exact amount of water vapour lost by the leaves
the number of stomata on a leaf

questions.solution_md: It measures uptake; since almost all absorbed water is transpired, this approximates the transpiration rate — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The shoot for a potometer is cut under water because

options.text_md: this makes the leaves open their stomata
this stops air from entering and blocking the xylem vessels
this washes dust off the leaves
this kills the cells at the cut end

questions.solution_md: An air bubble in the xylem would break the water column and stop uptake — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The reservoir of a potometer is used to

options.text_md: supply food to the shoot
measure the area of the leaves
push the air bubble back to the start of the scale before a new reading
trap carbon dioxide

questions.solution_md: Opening the stopcock lets water from the reservoir reset the bubble — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A fan is switched on near a potometer set up in still air. The air bubble will

options.text_md: move faster towards the shoot
stop moving
move away from the shoot
keep moving at the same speed

questions.solution_md: Wind removes humid air near the leaves, so transpiration and uptake speed up — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A potometer gives only an approximate value of the rate of transpiration.

**Reason (R):** A potometer measures the exact amount of water vapour released by the leaves.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is true. The reason is false: a potometer measures water uptake, not the vapour released — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The apparatus used to measure the rate of water uptake by a cut leafy shoot is Ganong's ______.
questions.solution_md: Potometer.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: the rate measured by a potometer is only roughly equal to the rate of transpiration.

answer.model_answer_md: It measures **water taken up**, and a small part of this is **used** in photosynthesis and kept in the cells, so uptake is not exactly equal to loss.

questions.solution_md: Uptake, not loss.

marking_scheme.step: Measures uptake; some water is used

questions.stem_md: State two limitations of Ganong's potometer.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It measures **water uptake**, not the actual **loss** of water vapour; some water is used by the shoot.
2. It uses a **cut shoot**, not a whole plant with roots, and readings are upset by **air leaks** or changes in temperature.

questions.solution_md: Uptake not loss; cut shoot and leaks.

questions.stem_md: Transpiration is slowest when the air around the plant is

options.text_md: dry and windy
humid and still
dry and still
warm and windy

questions.solution_md: Humid, still air keeps a moist layer around the leaf, so water vapour diffuses out slowly — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Transpiration increases in bright light mainly because

options.text_md: light makes the cuticle thinner
light increases the humidity of the air
light closes the stomata
the stomata open in light

questions.solution_md: Light opens stomata (and warms the leaf), so more water vapour escapes — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The leaves of Opuntia (a cactus) are reduced to spines. This helps the plant mainly by

options.text_md: reducing the surface from which water is lost
increasing the rate of transpiration
absorbing water from the air
making more food in the spines

questions.solution_md: Less leaf surface means far fewer stomata and less water loss; the green stem carries out photosynthesis — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Sunken stomata in desert plants reduce water loss mainly because

options.text_md: the pits fill with liquid water
moist air trapped in the pit above each stoma lowers the loss of water vapour
sunken stomata never open
the pits collect dew that the leaf absorbs

questions.solution_md: Still, humid air in the pit reduces the diffusion of water vapour out of the stoma — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Study the chart of potometer readings. Under which condition was water uptake fastest?

options.text_md: Still air, bright light
Still air, dark cupboard
Still air, shoot in a clear plastic bag
Fan blowing, bright light

questions.solution_md: The bubble moved fastest, 3 mm per minute, with the fan on — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A potometer with a leafy shoot is moved from a bright, dry, breezy balcony into a dark, steamy bathroom. What will happen to the bubble, and why?

options.text_md: It speeds up, because warm moist air increases evaporation
It does not change, because uptake does not depend on surroundings
It slows down greatly, because the stomata close in the dark and the humid, still air reduces evaporation
It moves away from the shoot, because the shoot gives out water

questions.solution_md: Three factors now all lower the rate: darkness closes stomata, high humidity and still air slow diffusion — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The rate of transpiration rises with a rise in temperature.

**Reason (R):** Most stomata of a dorsiventral leaf are on its lower surface.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the position of stomata does not explain the effect of temperature, which works by speeding evaporation — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Light, Humidity, Wind speed, Colour of the flowers.

answer.model_answer_md: **Colour of the flowers**; the others are **factors that affect the rate of transpiration**.

questions.solution_md: Flower colour has no effect.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: the leaves of a plant may droop on a hot, windy afternoon even though the soil is moist.

answer.model_answer_md: Water is **lost by transpiration faster than the roots can absorb** it, so the cells lose **turgor** and the leaves wilt.

questions.solution_md: Loss exceeds uptake.

marking_scheme.step: Loss faster than uptake; turgor lost

questions.stem_md: State two structural adaptations of desert plants that reduce transpiration.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Leaves reduced to spines** (as in cactus), so there is very little leaf surface.
2. A **thick waxy cuticle** and **sunken stomata**, which cut down the escape of water vapour.

questions.solution_md: Any two adaptations.

questions.stem_md: Explain how light, humidity and wind each affect the rate of transpiration.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Light:** stomata **open** in light, so transpiration **increases**; in darkness most stomata close.
**Humidity:** in humid air the leaf and air differ little in moisture, so water vapour diffuses out **more slowly**.
**Wind:** wind **blows away** the moist air near the leaf and keeps the outside dry, so transpiration **increases**.

questions.solution_md: Light up, humidity down, wind up.

questions.stem_md: Early on a humid morning, a row of tiny drops is seen along the tips and edges of grass leaves even though there was no rain or dew. The drops are due to

options.text_md: guttation through hydathodes
transpiration through stomata
bleeding from cut leaves
absorption of moisture from the air

questions.solution_md: When root pressure is high and transpiration is low, liquid water is pushed out through hydathodes — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Sap oozing from the cut stump of a freshly pruned vine is called

options.text_md: guttation
transpiration
wilting
bleeding

questions.solution_md: Bleeding is the flow of sap from a cut or injured part, driven by root pressure — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Guttation is most often seen at night and early in the morning.

**Reason (R):** At such times root pressure is high while transpiration is low.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and high root pressure with little transpiration is exactly what forces liquid water out — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The liquid given out in guttation is pure water.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. It contains dissolved mineral salts and some other substances, which may be left as a crust when it dries.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the loss of water in liquid form from the tips and margins of leaves.

answer.model_answer_md: **Guttation.**

questions.solution_md: Guttation.

questions.stem_md: Give two differences between guttation and transpiration.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. In **guttation** water is lost as **liquid drops**; in **transpiration** it is lost as **vapour**.
2. Guttation takes place through **hydathodes** at the leaf margins, mostly at night; transpiration takes place mainly through **stomata**, mostly by day.

questions.solution_md: Form; route and time.

questions.stem_md: What is bleeding in plants? State one way in which it differs from guttation.

answer.model_answer_md: **Bleeding** is the oozing of **sap from a cut or injured** part of a plant, caused by root pressure. It differs from guttation, which takes place from **uninjured leaves** through **hydathodes**.

questions.solution_md: Sap from wounds vs drops from hydathodes.

questions.passage_md: Tanvi set up two bell jars on glass plates in a sunny room. Under jar A she placed a watered potted plant; under jar B, a pot of watered soil with no plant. Both pots were wrapped in polythene. After three hours the inside of jar A was misty with drops, while jar B stayed clear.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Transpiration.**

**(b)** To stop water **evaporating from the soil and the pot**. Then any drops that form must come only from the **aerial parts of the plant**.

**(c)** It is the **control**. It is the same as A except that it has **no plant**, so it shows that the drops in A came from the **plant** and not from the soil, pot or air.

**(d)** **Fewer drops**, forming more slowly. In darkness most **stomata close**, so far **less water vapour** escapes from the leaves.

**(e)** (i) Touch the drops with **dry blue cobalt chloride paper** (or sprinkle **white anhydrous copper sulphate**): it turns **pink** (or **blue**), showing that the liquid is **water**. The process is important because it creates the **transpiration pull** that draws water and minerals up the stem (and it cools the leaves).

**OR** (ii) 1. **Wrap the pot and soil** completely in polythene so no water evaporates from them.
2. Make the bell jar **airtight** on the glass plate, for example with Vaseline at the rim.
3. Use a **dry** bell jar and keep both set-ups in the **same conditions** of light and temperature.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Transpiration.

**(b)** Prevents evaporation from soil.

**(c)** Control.

**(d)** Fewer drops: stomata closed.

**(e)** (i) Cobalt chloride turns pink; transpiration pull.

(ii) Three precautions.

questions.passage_md: Aman clipped strips of dry cobalt chloride paper, each covered by a glass slide, to the upper and lower surfaces of a leaf of a potted hibiscus plant. The paper on the lower surface changed colour in 2 minutes; the paper on the upper surface took 9 minutes. His teacher said a leaf of this kind has about 300 stomata per square millimetre on the lower surface and about 50 on the upper surface.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** From **blue** to **pink**.

**(b)** 6

**(c)** The lower surface has **many more stomata**, so **more water vapour** escapes from it in the same time. The paper there absorbs moisture faster and turns **pink** sooner.

**(d)** The slide keeps out **moisture from the surrounding air**, so the paper changes colour only because of water vapour coming **from the leaf**; it also holds the paper flat against the leaf.

**(e)** Cobalt chloride paper turns pink with **any** moisture. If it absorbed moisture from the air before use, it would already be **pink or partly pink**, and the result would be **unreliable**.

**(f)** (i) Both papers would turn pink at **about the same time**, because a maize leaf is **isobilateral** and has stomata in **nearly equal numbers** on both surfaces.

**OR** (ii) The lower paper would stay **blue much longer**, perhaps longer than the upper one, because the Vaseline **blocks the stomata** on that surface, so little water vapour can escape.

**(a)** Blue to pink.

**(b)** $300 \div 50 = 6$ times.

**(c)** More stomata, more vapour.

**(d)** Keeps out air moisture.

**(e)** Avoids false pink.

**(f)** (i) Same time: isobilateral.

(ii) Lower paper stays blue.

questions.passage_md:
A class used the apparatus shown to study a leafy shoot. They recorded how far the air bubble moved in 10 minutes under four conditions:

| Condition | Distance moved (mm) |
|---|---|
| Still air, bright light | 12 |
| Fan blowing, bright light | 30 |
| Still air, dark cupboard | 4 |
| Still air, shoot in a clear plastic bag | 5 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Ganong's potometer.**

**(b)** 1.2 mm per minute

**(c)** Wind **removes the moist air** next to the leaves, so water vapour diffuses out faster and **transpiration increases**. The shoot then **takes up water faster**, pulling the bubble along.

**(d)** In the **dark**, most **stomata close**, so little water is lost. Inside the **bag** the air soon becomes **humid**, so water vapour diffuses out slowly. In both, transpiration and therefore uptake fall.

**(e)** 4 cubic millimetres

**(f)** 1. Cut the shoot **under water** and fit it under water, so that **no air enters** the xylem.
2. Make every joint **airtight** with Vaseline, and keep the **temperature steady** while taking readings.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Potometer.

**(b)** $12 \div 10 = 1.2$ mm per minute.

**(c)** Wind increases transpiration.

**(d)** Stomata close; humid air.

children.stem_md: Name the apparatus.

answer.model_answer_md: **Ganong's potometer.**

children.stem_md: Calculate the rate of bubble movement in still air and bright light, in mm per minute.
Why did the bubble move faster when the fan was on?

answer.model_answer_md: Wind **removes the moist air** next to the leaves, so water vapour diffuses out faster and **transpiration increases**. The shoot then **takes up water faster**, pulling the bubble along.

children.stem_md: Why did the bubble move so slowly in the dark cupboard and inside the plastic bag?

answer.model_answer_md: In the **dark**, most **stomata close**, so little water is lost. Inside the **bag** the air soon becomes **humid**, so water vapour diffuses out slowly. In both, transpiration and therefore uptake fall.

children.stem_md: The capillary tube has a cross-section of 1 square millimetre. What volume of water (in cubic millimetres) did the shoot take up in 10 minutes in the dark?
State two precautions needed to get reliable readings with this apparatus.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Cut the shoot **under water** and fit it under water, so that **no air enters** the xylem.
2. Make every joint **airtight** with Vaseline, and keep the **temperature steady** while taking readings.

questions.passage_md:
Two flasks of water, each with a layer of oil on the water, held shoots of the same plant: flask A a leafy shoot and flask B a shoot with all its leaves removed. They were weighed at 9 a.m. and again at 5 p.m.:

| Flask | 9 a.m. (g) | 5 p.m. (g) |
|---|---|---|
| A (leafy) | 250.0 | 238.8 |
| B (leafless) | 231.4 | 230.6 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 11.2 g

**(b)** 1.4 g per hour

**(c)** To **stop evaporation** from the water surface, so that any loss in weight is due **only to water lost by the shoot**.

**(d)** Some water is lost from the **stem itself**, through its **cuticle** and any **lenticels** or young stomata on the stem, and a little may escape around the **cut ends** where the leaves were removed.

**(e)** Loss from A = 11.2 g; loss from B = 0.8 g. Water lost through the leaves ≈ 11.2 − 0.8 = **10.4 g**. Conclusion: plants lose water by **transpiration**, and most of it is lost through the **leaves**.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** 250.0 − 238.8 = 11.2 g.

**(b)** $11.2 \div 8 = 1.4$ g per hour.

**(c)** Stops evaporation.

**(d)** Loss through the stem.

**(e)** 10.4 g; leaves are the main site.

questions.passage_md: The figure shows the surface view of the same stoma on a leaf at noon and at midnight. Parts of the stoma at noon are lettered A to E.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Guard cell.**

**(b)** D is the **thick inner wall**. Because it **stretches less** than the thin outer wall, a turgid guard cell **curves outwards**, pulling the inner walls apart and **opening** the pore.

**(c)** At noon, in light, **potassium ions** move **into the guard cells** from the epidermal cells. Water follows by **osmosis**, the guard cells become **turgid** and curve apart: the pore opens. At midnight potassium ions move **out**, water leaves, the guard cells become **flaccid** and straight: the pore closes.

**(d)** Open stomata let **carbon dioxide** diffuse into the leaf for **photosynthesis**, which takes place only in light, and let **oxygen** out.

**(e)** E is an **epidermal cell**. A (the guard cell) is **bean-shaped** and contains **chloroplasts**, while E is irregular in shape and has **no chloroplasts**.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Guard cell.

**(b)** Unequal thickening.

**(c)** K+ in by day, out at night.

**(d)** Carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.

**(e)** Epidermal cell; chloroplasts.

children.stem_md: Name the cell labelled A.

answer.model_answer_md: **Guard cell.**

children.stem_md: State the role of the part labelled D in opening the stoma.

answer.model_answer_md: D is the **thick inner wall**. Because it **stretches less** than the thin outer wall, a turgid guard cell **curves outwards**, pulling the inner walls apart and **opening** the pore.

marking_scheme.step: Stretches less, so cell curves and pore opens

children.stem_md: Using the potassium ion exchange theory, explain why the stoma is open at noon and closed at midnight.

answer.model_answer_md: At noon, in light, **potassium ions** move **into the guard cells** from the epidermal cells. Water follows by **osmosis**, the guard cells become **turgid** and curve apart: the pore opens. At midnight potassium ions move **out**, water leaves, the guard cells become **flaccid** and straight: the pore closes.

children.solution_md: K+ in by day, out at night.

marking_scheme.step: K+ leaves at night; flaccid; closed

children.stem_md: How is the opening of stomata in daylight useful to the plant, besides allowing transpiration?

answer.model_answer_md: Open stomata let **carbon dioxide** diffuse into the leaf for **photosynthesis**, which takes place only in light, and let **oxygen** out.

children.stem_md: Name the cell E and give one way in which A differs from it.

answer.model_answer_md: E is an **epidermal cell**. A (the guard cell) is **bean-shaped** and contains **chloroplasts**, while E is irregular in shape and has **no chloroplasts**.

questions.stem_md: Read the following and answer the questions.
questions.passage_md: Meher keeps a cactus in a pot on a sunny windowsill and has a small lawn of grass. On humid mornings she sees tiny drops lined up along the tips of the grass blades, which vanish by mid-morning. On a hot, dry, windy afternoon she notices the lawn grass drooping slightly, while the cactus looks unchanged.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Guttation.**

**(b)** In the early morning **root pressure is high** and, because the air is humid and stomata are mostly closed, **transpiration is low**, so water is pushed out as drops through **hydathodes**. By afternoon transpiration is high and the drops do not form.

**(c)** Heat, dry air and wind made the grass **transpire very fast**. It **lost water faster than its roots could absorb** it, so its cells lost **turgor** and the blades wilted.

**(d)** 1. Its **leaves are reduced to spines**, so it has very little surface for transpiration.
2. Its fleshy green stem has a **thick waxy cuticle** and **few, sunken stomata**, and it stores water.

**(e)** (i) 1. **Form:** the grass loses **liquid drops**; the cactus loses water **vapour**.
2. **Route:** the drops come out through **hydathodes**; the vapour escapes through **stomata** (and cuticle).
3. **Time:** guttation happens at **night or early morning**; transpiration mostly by **day**. The drops also carry dissolved **salts**.

**OR** (ii) This is **bleeding**. 1. It occurs from a **cut or injured** part, while guttation occurs from **uninjured leaves**. 2. Bleeding releases **sap** from the cut tissues, while guttation releases drops through **hydathodes** at the leaf tips and margins.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Guttation.

**(b)** High root pressure, low transpiration.

**(c)** Loss exceeded uptake.

**(d)** Spines; thick cuticle and sunken stomata.

**(e)** (i) Form, route, time.

(ii) Bleeding; two differences.

children.stem_md: Name the process that produces the morning drops on the grass.

answer.model_answer_md: **Guttation.**

children.stem_md: Why are such drops seen in the early morning but not in the afternoon?

answer.model_answer_md: In the early morning **root pressure is high** and, because the air is humid and stomata are mostly closed, **transpiration is low**, so water is pushed out as drops through **hydathodes**. By afternoon transpiration is high and the drops do not form.

children.stem_md: Why did the grass droop on the hot, windy afternoon?

answer.model_answer_md: Heat, dry air and wind made the grass **transpire very fast**. It **lost water faster than its roots could absorb** it, so its cells lost **turgor** and the blades wilted.

children.stem_md: State two features of the cactus that help it to survive the same conditions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Its **leaves are reduced to spines**, so it has very little surface for transpiration.
2. Its fleshy green stem has a **thick waxy cuticle** and **few, sunken stomata**, and it stores water.

children.solution_md: Spines; thick cuticle and sunken stomata.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Give three differences between the drops seen on the grass and the water lost by the cactus.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Form:** the grass loses **liquid drops**; the cactus loses water **vapour**.
2. **Route:** the drops come out through **hydathodes**; the vapour escapes through **stomata** (and cuticle).
3. **Time:** guttation happens at **night or early morning**; transpiration mostly by **day**. The drops also carry dissolved **salts**.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Meher cuts a stem of a rose bush and sees sap oozing from the cut end of the plant. Name this process and give two ways in which it differs from what she saw on the grass.

answer.model_answer_md: This is **bleeding**. 1. It occurs from a **cut or injured** part, while guttation occurs from **uninjured leaves**. 2. Bleeding releases **sap** from the cut tissues, while guttation releases drops through **hydathodes** at the leaf tips and margins.
